label: Curvature of Riemannian Manifolds
notes: This appendix to part II.1 builds the bridge between smooth Riemannian curvature and the metric curvature bounds of CAT(k) theory. The whole point is that sectional curvature, a tensorial invariant, controls how geodesic triangles spread, and that spreading is exactly what Alexandrov comparison measures intrinsically.

label: Two Languages for Curvature
notes: Set up the dictionary the appendix translates. On one side sits the smooth Riemannian world with its metric tensor, Levi-Civita connection, and curvature tensor. On the other sits the synthetic metric world of geodesic spaces and comparison triangles. The appendix shows these two languages describe the same geometry.

label: The Riemann Curvature Tensor
notes: Recall the curvature tensor as the failure of second covariant derivatives to commute. Stress that R measures path dependence of parallel transport around an infinitesimal loop, and that all its symmetries let us extract a single number from any tangent two-plane. Keep this tensorial, but anchored to transport intuition.

label: Sectional Curvature of a 2-Plane
notes: Define sectional curvature by feeding the curvature tensor an orthonormal pair spanning a tangent plane. Emphasize that K depends only on the plane sigma, not the chosen basis, and that in dimension two it reduces to Gauss curvature. This scalar is the invariant the comparison theory reads.

label: Curvature as Geodesic Spreading
notes: Give the kinematic meaning. Fire a fan of geodesics from a point inside a two-plane and watch nearby rays. Positive sectional curvature focuses them back together, negative curvature drives them apart faster than in flat space. This converging-versus-spreading picture is the visual heart of the appendix.

label: Jacobi Fields Quantify Spreading
notes: Make the spreading precise with Jacobi fields. The Jacobi equation has the sectional curvature as its coefficient, so the sign of K directly governs whether the separation between neighbouring geodesics grows or shrinks. This is the analytic engine behind every comparison estimate that follows.

label: Model Spaces M_k
notes: Recall the comparison models. For each real k there is a complete simply connected surface of constant curvature k: the sphere when k is positive, the Euclidean plane at zero, and the hyperbolic plane scaled when k is negative. Triangles in the manifold are compared against triangles drawn in M_k.

label: Comparison Triangles in M_k
notes: Explain the comparison triangle construction. Given a geodesic triangle in the manifold, build the triangle in M_k with the same three side lengths. CAT(k) compares chord distances inside the real triangle against the corresponding chords of this model triangle. The inequality direction encodes the curvature bound.

label: Rauch and the Upper Bound
notes: State the Rauch comparison theorem as the local engine. Bounding sectional curvature above by k controls Jacobi field growth from below, which forces geodesics to spread no slower than in M_k. Locally this makes triangles at least as thin as their comparison triangles, the defining CAT(k) inequality.

label: Toponogov and Thin Triangles
notes: Present the equivalence as a thin-triangle statement. Sectional curvature at most k is equivalent, locally, to every geodesic triangle being thinner than its M_k comparison triangle. Toponogov's globalization upgrades the local estimate to a global one under completeness, matching the metric CAT(k) definition exactly.

label: Curvature Bounded Below
notes: Cover the reverse inequality. Sectional curvature at least k corresponds to triangles being fatter than the M_k model, the Alexandrov notion of curvature bounded below. Flip every comparison inequality. Stress that the two one-sided theories are genuinely different and that this appendix focuses on the upper bound feeding CAT(k).

label: Smooth NPC = Smooth CAT(0)
notes: Land the headline. A smooth Riemannian manifold has nonpositive sectional curvature if and only if it is locally CAT(0). This embeds classical Hadamard manifold geometry inside the synthetic metric theory, so every CAT(0) theorem specializes to nonpositively curved manifolds while extending to singular spaces beyond them.
